newsitem.title: USA: Utility hopes Net, phone, cable will spark revenues.
newsitem.headline: Utility hopes Net, phone, cable will spark revenues.

text.p: Boston Edison and a start-up telecommunications company Monday announced a $300 million joint venture to provide Internet access, cable television and phone service to the Boston area over the utility's fiber optic network.
"We're looking to give the customer one-stop shopping," said a Boston Edison spokesman.
The joint venture is one of the consequences of the watershed deregulation of the electrical power and telecommunications industries.
Financial analysts said the venture was an attempt to exploit what Boston Edison Chief Executive Officer Tom May described as the fourth largest fiber optic network in Massachusetts.

Boston Edison uses only 10 percent to 20 percent of the network, said Prudential Securities Research Analyst Barry Abramson. "That leaves 80 to 90 percent of that network available for partners," he said.
The joint venture gives telecommunications firm RCN Inc. about 200 miles of fiber optic cable and right of ways to build more fiber optic networks to serve Boston Edison customers.
Boston Edison and Boston-based RCN said they planned to invest $300 million in the venture over the next five years.
RCN, a subsidiary of Princeton, N.J.-based telecommunications company C-TEC Corp., is already providing some telecommunication services in New York and parts of Boston.
The landmark telecommunications act signed in February tore down the barriers that kept local phone and long-distance phone service and cable TV separate.
RCN and Boston Edison want to capture new business from 30 percent of the utility's 1.6 million customers in the greater Boston area.

The venture aims to attract customers who now get phone service from NYNEX Corp. and cable TV from Cablevision Systems Corp. in the Boston area, "two established players: one with a 100-year-old network and the other a 20- to 30-year-old network," said C-TEC Chief Executive David McCourt.
Like other utilities, Boston Edison is facing increased competition as electricity becomes a deregulated commodity, which will take place in Massachusetts in January 1998.
Regulators and the industry say competition promises cheaper power for a region whose energy costs are among the highest in the nation.
Boston Edison, like others, is trying to find a way to replace revenues expected to be lost once its protected regulated status changes.

Analyst Douglas Fischer of A.G. Edwards said, "There are a number of different ways electric utilities can take advantage of their strengths -- their fiber optic networks, their right of ways -- and this is one of them."
